breakfast.name: Loco Moco
ingredients: Brown gravy (made from pan drippings, soy sauce, and beef broth)
instructions: Loco moco is the iconic Hawaiian plate breakfast -- rice, burger patty, gravy, fried egg
Steam short grain white rice until sticky
Form ground beef into a thick patty and pan-fry in a hot skillet until browned
Make brown gravy from the pan drippings with beef broth, soy sauce, and Worcestershire
Fry an egg sunny side up -- the runny yolk is essential
Layer: rice on the bottom, then patty, then gravy poured over, then the egg on top
Garnish with sliced green onion
Invented at Lincoln Grill in Hilo in 1949 -- a dish born from local kids wanting something cheap and filling
breakfast.description: Iconic Hawaiian plate breakfast -- loco moco. White rice topped with a beef patty, brown gravy, and a sunny-side-up fried egg. Invented at Lincoln Grill in Hilo (1949). Cheap, filling, and a staple at every plate lunch spot in the islands.

breakfast.name: Spam Musubi
ingredients: Sushi rice (short grain, seasoned with rice vinegar and sugar)
Musubi mold (or use the Spam can)
instructions: Spam musubi is the quintessential Hawaiian snack-breakfast -- Spam, rice, nori
Slice Spam into rectangular pieces about 1/4 inch thick
Pan-fry the Spam slices in soy sauce and sugar until caramelized and slightly crispy
Press seasoned sushi rice into a musubi mold (or the cleaned-out Spam can)
Place caramelized Spam on top of the rice block
Wrap a strip of nori around the whole thing, sealing with a dab of water
Spam musubi is sold at every gas station, convenience store, and ABC Store in Hawaii
Hawaii consumes more Spam per capita than any other US state -- a legacy of World War II military rations
breakfast.description: Quintessential Hawaiian snack -- spam musubi, caramelized Spam on pressed sushi rice wrapped in nori. Hawaii consumes more Spam per capita than any other US state (a WWII military rations legacy). Sold at every gas station and ABC Store in the islands.

breakfast.name: Portuguese Sausage, Eggs, and Rice
instructions: Portuguese sausage and eggs is the standard Hawaiian diner breakfast
Slice linguica (Portuguese sausage) into thick rounds and pan-fry until the edges crisp
The sausage is garlicky, slightly spicy, and pork-based -- brought by Portuguese plantation workers
Fry or scramble eggs alongside
Serve with two scoops of white rice (not toast -- rice is the Hawaiian breakfast starch)
A splash of Tabasco or homemade chili pepper water on the side
Every plate lunch spot in Hawaii serves this -- it is the default morning order
breakfast.description: Standard Hawaiian diner breakfast -- Portuguese sausage (linguica), fried eggs, and two scoops rice. Linguica was brought by Portuguese plantation workers in the 1800s. Every plate lunch spot serves this as the default morning order.

breakfast.name: Acai Bowl
ingredients: Fresh tropical fruit (mango, papaya, strawberries, banana slices)
instructions: Acai bowls are the modern Hawaiian breakfast -- thick frozen acai blended into a smoothie bowl
Blend frozen acai packets with frozen banana and a splash of coconut milk until thick
The consistency should be thicker than a smoothie -- spoonable, not drinkable
Pour into a bowl and top with granola, fresh fruit, shredded coconut, and a drizzle of honey
Every surf town in Hawaii has an acai bowl shop -- it became a Hawaiian staple in the 2000s
The acai berry itself is from Brazil -- but Hawaii made the bowl its own
breakfast.description: Modern Hawaiian breakfast -- acai bowl, thick blended acai topped with granola, fresh tropical fruit, shredded coconut, and honey. Every surf town has an acai shop. The Brazilian acai berry became a Hawaiian staple in the 2000s.

breakfast.name: Hawaiian Sweet Bread French Toast
ingredients: Hawaiian sweet bread (King's Hawaiian or homemade)
Coconut syrup or tropical fruit compote
instructions: Hawaiian sweet bread French toast -- the soft, slightly sweet bread soaks up the custard beautifully
Whisk eggs with coconut milk, vanilla, and cinnamon
Slice Hawaiian sweet bread thick -- about 1 inch
Soak each slice in the coconut custard until saturated
Cook on a buttered griddle until golden on both sides
Top with coconut syrup or a compote of mango and lilikoi (passion fruit)
King's Hawaiian bread was created by Robert Taira in Hilo in the 1950s -- a Japanese-Hawaiian baker blending Portuguese sweet bread traditions with island flavors
breakfast.description: Hawaiian sweet bread French toast -- thick slices of the soft, slightly sweet bread soaked in coconut custard and griddled golden. King's Hawaiian was created by Robert Taira in Hilo (1950s) -- a Japanese-Hawaiian baker blending Portuguese sweet bread with island flavors.

lunch.name: Plate Lunch
ingredients: Protein: teriyaki chicken, kalua pork, or katsu
Macaroni salad (Hawaiian-style with Best Foods mayo)
instructions: The plate lunch is the format that defines Hawaiian food culture
Two scoops of white rice -- always two scoops, this is non-negotiable
One scoop of Hawaiian-style macaroni salad -- creamy, simple, with Best Foods mayo (not Hellmann's)
One protein: teriyaki chicken, kalua pork, katsu, or mahi mahi
Served on a divided plate or in a styrofoam container
Descended from the bento boxes that Japanese plantation workers brought to the sugar fields
Every ethnic group's food adapted to the plate lunch format: Korean, Filipino, Japanese, Hawaiian
The plate lunch is Hawaii's contribution to American food culture -- portable, generous, multicultural
lunch.description: The format that defines Hawaiian food culture -- plate lunch. Two scoops rice, one scoop Hawaiian mac salad, and a protein (teriyaki chicken, kalua pork, katsu). Descended from Japanese plantation bento boxes. Hawaii's contribution to American food: portable, generous, multicultural.

lunch.name: Poke Bowl
instructions: Poke is the original Hawaiian raw fish preparation -- not the mainland fast-casual version
Cube sashimi-grade ahi tuna into bite-sized pieces
Traditional Hawaiian poke: just fish, sea salt, limu (seaweed), inamona (candlenut)
Shoyu poke: cubed ahi dressed in soy sauce, sesame oil, green onion -- the most popular style
The fish must be fresh -- in Hawaii, poke is made from fish caught that day
Serve over rice or eat it straight from the bowl
Poke has been eaten in Hawaii for centuries -- the word means "to slice" or "to cut" in Hawaiian
The mainland poke bowl trend (2010s) diverged significantly from traditional Hawaiian poke
At a Hawaiian poke counter, you pick your fish from a deli case -- it is sold by the pound
lunch.description: Original Hawaiian raw fish preparation -- poke. Cubed ahi tuna with soy sauce, sesame oil, green onion, and limu (seaweed). The word means "to slice" in Hawaiian. Eaten for centuries. The mainland poke bowl trend diverged significantly from the traditional Hawaiian version.

lunch.name: Garlic Shrimp (Giovanni's Style)
instructions: Garlic shrimp is the iconic North Shore food truck dish
Use shell-on shrimp -- eating with your hands and peeling is part of the experience
Use an enormous amount of garlic -- at least a full head per pound of shrimp
Saute garlic in a mix of butter and olive oil until fragrant but not burnt
Add shrimp and cook until pink, tossing in the garlicky butter
Squeeze lemon juice over the top
Serve on a paper plate with two scoops of rice -- scoop the garlic butter sauce over the rice
Giovanni's Aloha Shrimp Truck on the North Shore of Oahu started this in 1993
The line at the truck is always long -- that is part of the North Shore experience
lunch.description: Iconic North Shore food truck dish -- garlic shrimp. Shell-on shrimp sauteed in an enormous amount of garlic and butter. Giovanni's Aloha Shrimp Truck on the North Shore of Oahu started this (1993). The long line is part of the experience.

lunch.name: Kalua Pig
ingredients: Ti leaves or banana leaves (for wrapping)
instructions: Kalua pig is the centerpiece of the Hawaiian luau -- whole pig cooked in an underground imu (earth oven)
Traditional method: dig a pit, line with hot rocks, wrap the whole pig in ti leaves, bury it
Home method: rub pork shoulder with Hawaiian sea salt and liquid smoke
Slow cook at 300F for 8 hours (or in a slow cooker for 16 hours) until falling apart
Shred the meat with two forks -- it should pull apart effortlessly
The smoky, salty, tender pork is the most important dish at any Hawaiian gathering
Serve with shredded cabbage
Kalua means "to cook in an underground oven" -- it refers to the cooking method, not the meat
Liquid smoke is the home cook's substitute for the imu -- not traditional, but widely accepted
lunch.description: Centerpiece of the Hawaiian luau -- kalua pig. Pork shoulder rubbed with Hawaiian sea salt, slow-cooked until falling apart and smoky. Traditionally cooked in an imu (underground oven) wrapped in ti leaves. Kalua means "to cook in an underground oven" -- the method, not the meat.

lunch.name: Manapua (Hawaiian Char Siu Bao)
ingredients: Flour, sugar, yeast, baking powder (for dough)
Char siu pork (diced -- sweet BBQ pork)
instructions: Manapua is Hawaii's version of Chinese char siu bao -- steamed or baked pork buns
The name comes from "mea ono puaa" -- delicious pork thing -- in Hawaiian
Hawaiian manapua are larger than dim sum char siu bao -- bigger, fluffier, more filling
The dough: a soft, slightly sweet yeast dough that puffs up during steaming
Fill with diced char siu pork mixed with oyster sauce and sesame oil
Steam for 15-20 minutes until the buns are puffy and the filling is hot
Manapua men used to drive trucks through neighborhoods selling hot buns -- like an ice cream truck
The most famous manapua shop: Royal Kitchen in Honolulu's Chinatown
Modern fillings include curry chicken, kalua pig, and even pizza
lunch.description: Hawaii's version of Chinese char siu bao -- manapua, large steamed pork buns. The name is from Hawaiian: "mea ono puaa" (delicious pork thing). Larger and fluffier than dim sum bao. Manapua men drove trucks through neighborhoods selling hot buns. Royal Kitchen in Chinatown is the most famous shop.

lunch.name: Laulau
instructions: Laulau is traditional Hawaiian food -- pork and fish wrapped in taro and ti leaves, steamed
Layer taro leaves (luau leaves) and place cubes of salted pork and butterfish inside
Wrap the bundle in ti leaves -- the ti leaves are not eaten, they are the wrapper
Steam for 4-6 hours until the taro leaves are silky and the pork is tender
The taro leaves cook down and become like spinach -- soft, earthy, slightly mineral
Laulau is one of the few surviving pre-contact Hawaiian cooking methods
The combination of pork and fish in the same bundle creates a unique umami
Modern laulau can also be made with chicken or just fish for a lighter version
lunch.description: Traditional Hawaiian food -- laulau. Pork and salted butterfish wrapped in taro (luau) leaves, then wrapped in ti leaves and steamed for hours. The taro leaves cook down silky and earthy. One of the few surviving pre-contact Hawaiian cooking methods.

dinner.name: Huli Huli Chicken
instructions: Huli huli chicken is Hawaiian rotisserie chicken -- "huli" means "turn" in Hawaiian
Make the glaze: soy sauce, brown sugar, ketchup, ginger, garlic, pineapple juice, sesame oil
Marinate chicken for at least 2 hours (overnight is better)
Grill over medium heat, turning (huli!) and basting with glaze repeatedly
The chicken should be deeply caramelized, slightly charred, and sticky
Invented by Ernest Morgado on Oahu in 1955 for a fundraiser
Huli huli chicken fundraisers are a Hawaiian institution -- churches, schools, and sports teams all do them
The smoke from the grills and the sweet-salty glaze aroma is the smell of a Hawaiian weekend
dinner.description: Hawaiian rotisserie chicken -- huli huli, marinated in soy sauce, brown sugar, pineapple juice, and ginger, grilled while turning ("huli" means "turn" in Hawaiian). Invented by Ernest Morgado (1955). Huli huli fundraisers are a Hawaiian institution -- churches, schools, sports teams.

dinner.name: Shoyu Chicken
instructions: Shoyu chicken is the everyday Hawaiian comfort dinner -- chicken braised in sweetened soy sauce
Combine soy sauce, brown sugar, sliced ginger, garlic, and star anise in a pot
Add chicken thighs skin-side down and bring to a simmer
Braise on low heat for 35-40 minutes, turning once
The sauce reduces into a glossy, sweet-salty glaze
Shoyu chicken is the dish that every local kid grew up eating
The Japanese influence is clear -- teriyaki and shoyu chicken share the same flavor family
Serve over white rice with the reduced sauce poured on top
dinner.description: Everyday Hawaiian comfort dinner -- shoyu chicken, chicken thighs braised in sweetened soy sauce with ginger, garlic, and star anise. The sauce reduces into a glossy sweet-salty glaze. The dish every local kid grew up eating. Japanese influence in the teriyaki flavor family.

dinner.name: Chicken Katsu
instructions: Chicken katsu is the Japanese-Hawaiian fried cutlet -- a plate lunch staple
Pound chicken breasts to even thickness (about 1/2 inch)
Dredge in flour, dip in beaten egg, coat generously with panko
Fry in hot oil (350F) until golden and crispy -- about 4 minutes per side
Slice into strips and serve with tonkatsu sauce
Chicken katsu is served at every plate lunch spot alongside the teriyaki and kalua pig
The Japanese katsu became Hawaiian through the plantation era -- Japanese workers brought the technique
Kids in Hawaii grow up eating chicken katsu the way mainland kids eat chicken nuggets
dinner.description: Japanese-Hawaiian fried cutlet -- chicken katsu. Panko-crusted chicken breast fried golden, sliced, and served with tonkatsu sauce. A plate lunch staple. Japanese plantation workers brought the technique. Kids in Hawaii eat chicken katsu the way mainland kids eat nuggets.

dinner.name: Luau Stew (Squid Luau)
instructions: Luau stew (or squid luau) is a traditional Hawaiian dish -- squid cooked with taro leaves and coconut milk
Clean the squid and cut into rings
Cook taro leaves with water until tender -- this takes about an hour (taro leaves must be fully cooked)
Taro leaves contain calcium oxalate that must be broken down by cooking -- never eat them raw
Add coconut milk, cooked squid, and butter
Simmer until the squid is tender and the stew is creamy
The combination of coconut, taro greens, and seafood is fundamentally Hawaiian
The word "luau" originally referred to the taro leaf, not the party -- the feast was named after the food
dinner.description: Traditional Hawaiian stew -- squid luau, squid cooked with taro (luau) leaves and coconut milk. The word "luau" originally referred to the taro leaf, not the party. Taro leaves must be fully cooked to break down calcium oxalate. Fundamentally Hawaiian: coconut, taro greens, seafood.

dinner.name: Lomi-Lomi Salmon
ingredients: Crushed ice (mixed in to keep cold)
instructions: Lomi-lomi salmon is a Hawaiian side dish -- salt-cured salmon mixed with tomato and onion
"Lomi" means "to massage" in Hawaiian -- the ingredients are gently mixed by hand
Salt-cure the salmon overnight in Hawaiian sea salt, then rinse and dice
Combine with diced tomato, sweet Maui onion, and green onion
Mix gently with your hands (lomi lomi)
Serve cold, often with crushed ice mixed in to keep it chilled
Lomi-lomi salmon appears at every luau and Hawaiian gathering
Salmon is not native to Hawaii -- it arrived with early Western traders and was preserved with salt
The tomato-onion-fish combination echoes ceviche but uses salt-cured fish instead of citrus-cured
dinner.description: Hawaiian side dish -- lomi-lomi salmon, salt-cured salmon mixed ("lomi" means "to massage") with diced tomato and sweet Maui onion, served cold. Salmon is not native to Hawaii -- it arrived with Western traders and was preserved with salt. Appears at every luau.

dinner.name: Chicken Long Rice
instructions: Chicken long rice is a Hawaiian-Chinese comfort dish -- chicken and bean thread noodles in ginger broth
Simmer chicken thighs in broth with ginger and garlic until cooked through
Remove chicken, shred the meat, return to the broth
Add soaked long rice (bean thread noodles) and cook until the noodles are translucent
Season with sea salt, sesame oil, and top with sliced green onion
Chicken long rice is a luau staple and a cold-weather comfort food
The Chinese noodle tradition adapted to Hawaiian tastes -- simpler, ginger-forward
"Long rice" is the Hawaiian name for glass noodles or bean thread noodles
dinner.description: Hawaiian-Chinese comfort dish -- chicken long rice, shredded chicken and bean thread noodles in ginger broth. Long rice is the Hawaiian name for glass noodles. A luau staple and cold-weather comfort food. Chinese noodle tradition adapted to Hawaiian tastes -- simpler and ginger-forward.

snacks.name: Malasadas
instructions: Malasadas are Portuguese doughnuts -- brought to Hawaii by Madeiran plantation workers
Make a rich yeast dough with eggs, butter, milk, and evaporated milk
Let rise until doubled (about 1-2 hours)
Pull off pieces and stretch into balls -- do not use a cutter, they are hand-shaped
Deep fry at 350F until puffed and golden brown on all sides
Roll immediately in sugar while still hot
Leonard's Bakery in Honolulu (opened 1952) made malasadas famous beyond the Portuguese community
Malasada Day is Shrove Tuesday (Fat Tuesday) in Hawaii -- bakeries sell out
Modern fillings: haupia (coconut pudding), custard, guava, ube (purple yam)
snacks.description: Portuguese doughnuts brought by Madeiran plantation workers -- malasadas, hand-shaped yeasted dough balls deep-fried and rolled in sugar. Leonard's Bakery (Honolulu, 1952) made them famous. Malasada Day is Shrove Tuesday in Hawaii. Modern fillings: haupia, custard, guava, ube.

snacks.name: Li Hing Mui Snacks
ingredients: Li hing mui powder (dried plum powder)
Fresh fruit: mango, pineapple, or watermelon
Or gummy bears, dried mango, arare (rice crackers)
instructions: Li hing mui powder is the distinctively Hawaiian-Chinese flavor -- salty, sour, sweet plum powder
Sprinkle li hing mui powder on fresh cut mango, pineapple, or watermelon
Also used on gummy bears, dried fruit, and arare (Japanese rice crackers)
The flavor profile: salty, tangy, sweet, slightly licorice-like -- addictive
Li hing mui is derived from Chinese preserved plum -- the powder is ground from dried plums
Tourists either love it or find it baffling -- there is no mainland equivalent
Li hing mui margaritas, li hing mui lemonade, li hing mui everything -- Hawaii puts it on everything
snacks.description: Distinctively Hawaiian-Chinese flavor -- li hing mui, salty-sour-sweet dried plum powder sprinkled on fresh fruit, gummy bears, and arare. Derived from Chinese preserved plum. Tourists either love it or find it baffling. Hawaii puts li hing mui on everything.

snacks.name: Arare (Japanese Rice Crackers)
ingredients: Arare mix (kakimochi -- assorted Japanese rice crackers)
instructions: Arare (kakimochi) is the Japanese rice cracker snack mix that every Hawaiian household keeps on hand
The homemade version: toss arare crackers in a glaze of melted butter, soy sauce, sugar, and Worcestershire
Bake low and slow until crispy and glazed
Hawaiian arare mix is sweeter and more buttery than Japanese originals
Known as "mochi crunch" or "kakimochi" -- it is the default party snack in Hawaii
Japanese plantation workers brought arare to Hawaii -- it adapted to local tastes
Often mixed with furikake-seasoned Chex mix for a Hawaiian party snack mix
snacks.description: Japanese rice cracker snack -- arare (kakimochi), tossed in melted butter, soy sauce, sugar, and Worcestershire, baked crispy. Every Hawaiian household keeps it on hand. Sweeter and more buttery than Japanese originals. The default party snack.

snacks.name: Musubi Varieties
instructions: Beyond classic Spam musubi, Hawaii has a whole musubi culture
Hot dog musubi: a glazed hot dog on rice, wrapped in nori
Bacon musubi: crispy bacon strips on rice with furikake
Egg musubi: thin omelet folded over rice
Furikake musubi: rice mixed with furikake, no protein -- the simplest version
Musubi is the on-the-go snack of Hawaii -- eaten for breakfast, lunch, snack, any time
ABC Stores, 7-Eleven, and gas stations all have musubi warmers by the register
The musubi warmer is as Hawaiian as the shave ice stand
snacks.description: Hawaiian musubi culture beyond classic Spam -- hot dog musubi, bacon musubi, egg musubi, furikake musubi. On-the-go snack eaten any time of day. ABC Stores, 7-Eleven, and gas stations all have musubi warmers by the register.

snacks.name: Poi
instructions: Poi is the most culturally significant Hawaiian food -- mashed taro root
Cook taro root until very soft, then mash and mix with water to desired consistency
Fresh poi (one-finger poi) is thick enough to eat with one finger
Day-old poi ferments slightly and becomes more sour -- some prefer this tangy "sour poi"
Taro (kalo) is the elder sibling of the Hawaiian people in creation mythology
Poi is considered sacred in Hawaiian culture -- arguments stop when the poi bowl is uncovered
Poi is naturally gluten-free, hypoallergenic, and easily digestible
The starchy, slightly sweet, slightly sour flavor is an acquired taste for non-Hawaiians
Poi is traditionally eaten alongside all other Hawaiian foods -- it is the starch, not a side dish
snacks.description: Most culturally significant Hawaiian food -- poi, mashed taro (kalo) root. Taro is the elder sibling of the Hawaiian people in creation mythology. Arguments stop when the poi bowl is uncovered. Naturally gluten-free and hypoallergenic. An acquired taste for non-Hawaiians.

desserts.name: Haupia
instructions: Haupia is the Hawaiian coconut pudding -- served at every luau and local celebration
Combine coconut milk, sugar, and cornstarch (dissolved in water)
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until thick
Pour into a flat pan and refrigerate until set (about 2-4 hours)
Cut into squares -- haupia is firm enough to pick up with your fingers
The texture: somewhere between Jell-O and flan -- firm but jiggly
Haupia is traditionally the dessert at a luau -- it ends the meal
Modern: haupia pie (a chocolate-haupia layered pie from Ted's Bakery is legendary)
The flavor is pure coconut -- simple and not overly sweet
desserts.description: Hawaiian coconut pudding -- haupia, coconut milk thickened with starch, chilled, and cut into squares. Firm enough to pick up with your fingers. The traditional luau dessert. Ted's Bakery's chocolate-haupia layered pie is legendary. Pure coconut flavor, not overly sweet.

imageCredit.author: Arnold Gatilao from Fremont, CA, USA

desserts.name: Butter Mochi
instructions: Butter mochi is the Hawaiian dessert bar -- chewy, buttery, coconut-rich
Mix mochiko flour with sugar, baking powder, eggs, coconut milk, evaporated milk, melted butter, and vanilla
Pour into a buttered 9x13 pan
Bake at 350F for about 1 hour until the top is golden and a toothpick comes out clean
Let cool completely, then cut into squares
The texture: dense, chewy, and sticky -- the mochiko flour creates the characteristic mochi chew
Butter mochi is a potluck and bake sale staple in Hawaii
Japanese mochi technique meets American butter and evaporated milk -- a true Hawaiian fusion
Variations: ube (purple yam) butter mochi, macadamia nut butter mochi
desserts.description: Hawaiian dessert bar -- butter mochi, chewy-buttery-coconut-rich squares made with mochiko (sweet rice flour). Japanese mochi technique meets American butter and evaporated milk -- true Hawaiian fusion. A potluck and bake sale staple. Variations: ube, macadamia nut.

desserts.name: Shave Ice
ingredients: Block ice (shaved into fine snow -- not crushed)
Flavored syrups: lilikoi (passion fruit), guava, mango, blue vanilla, li hing mui
Mochi balls, azuki beans, or haupia (bottom add-ins)
Ice cream scoop (optional, at the bottom)
instructions: Shave ice (not "shaved" -- the Hawaiian term drops the d) is the island's iconic frozen treat
The ice is shaved from a block into fine, fluffy snow -- NOT crushed or crunched
The fineness of the shave is what separates good shave ice from a mainland snow cone
Choose 2-3 syrup flavors: lilikoi, guava, mango, coconut, blue vanilla, li hing mui
Add-ins at the bottom: a scoop of ice cream, mochi balls, or sweet azuki beans
Top with a "snow cap" of sweetened condensed milk
Matsumoto's on the North Shore of Oahu has had a line out the door since 1951
Shave ice came from Japanese kakigori -- plantation workers adapted it
A rainbow shave ice (strawberry, lemon, blue vanilla) is the classic tourist order
desserts.description: Hawaii's iconic frozen treat -- shave ice (not "shaved"). Block ice shaved into fine fluffy snow (NOT crushed), topped with tropical syrups (lilikoi, guava, mango), a snow cap of condensed milk, and add-ins like mochi and azuki beans. Came from Japanese kakigori. Matsumoto's North Shore has had a line since 1951.

desserts.name: Coconut Haupia Pie
ingredients: Chocolate layer: dark chocolate, coconut milk, sugar
Haupia layer: coconut milk, sugar, cornstarch
instructions: Coconut haupia pie is a layered chocolate and coconut cream pie -- Ted's Bakery made it famous
Make a chocolate ganache layer with dark chocolate and coconut milk
Pour into a pre-baked pie crust and let set slightly
Make a haupia layer on top: coconut milk thickened with cornstarch and sugar
Refrigerate until both layers are set
Top with whipped cream
Ted's Bakery on the North Shore of Oahu created this -- it became legendary
The chocolate and coconut layers create a perfect sweet-rich balance
Every bakery in Hawaii now makes a version -- but Ted's is the original
desserts.description: Layered chocolate and coconut cream pie -- haupia pie, made famous by Ted's Bakery on the North Shore of Oahu. Dark chocolate ganache on the bottom, haupia (coconut pudding) on top, whipped cream. Every bakery in Hawaii makes a version -- Ted's is the original.

imageCredit.author: Arnold Gatilao from Fremont, CA, USA

desserts.name: Kulolo (Hawaiian Taro Pudding)
instructions: Kulolo is a traditional Hawaiian taro pudding -- dense, sweet, and earthy
Grate raw taro very finely
Mix with coconut milk and brown sugar
Wrap in ti leaves and steam for 3-4 hours (or bake wrapped in foil)
The long cooking transforms the starchy taro into a dense, fudgy pudding
Kulolo is traditionally made for special occasions and luaus
The flavor: deeply earthy from taro, sweet from coconut and sugar, slightly smoky from ti leaves
One of the oldest Hawaiian desserts -- predates Western contact
desserts.description: Traditional Hawaiian taro pudding -- kulolo, finely grated taro mixed with coconut milk and sugar, steamed in ti leaves for hours. Dense and fudgy. One of the oldest Hawaiian desserts -- predates Western contact. Made for luaus and special occasions.

drinks.name: POG Juice
instructions: POG is the Hawaiian juice blend -- Passion fruit, Orange, Guava
Mix equal parts (or to taste) passion fruit, orange, and guava juices
The combination is tangy, sweet, and tropical -- the quintessential Hawaiian drink
Created by Mary Soon at Haleakala Dairy on Maui in 1971
POG (or POG juice) is served at every hotel breakfast buffet, school cafeteria, and restaurant in Hawaii
The POG game (pogs/milk caps) that swept the 1990s was named after these juice bottle caps
drinks.description: Hawaiian juice blend -- POG, Passion fruit, Orange, Guava. Created by Mary Soon at Haleakala Dairy on Maui (1971). Served at every hotel breakfast, school cafeteria, and restaurant in Hawaii. The 1990s POG game was named after these juice bottle caps.

drinks.name: Lilikoi Lemonade
instructions: Lilikoi lemonade is a Hawaiian twist on classic lemonade -- passion fruit meets citrus
Scoop out fresh lilikoi pulp (seeds and all) or use frozen concentrate
Combine with fresh lemon juice, sugar, and water
Stir until sugar dissolves, serve over ice
Lilikoi (passion fruit) grows wild in Hawaii -- vines cover fences and trees
The flavor: intensely tart, floral, and tropical
Lilikoi lemonade is the house drink at many Hawaiian restaurants and food trucks
drinks.description: Hawaiian twist on lemonade -- lilikoi lemonade, passion fruit mixed with fresh lemon. Lilikoi grows wild in Hawaii, covering fences and trees. Intensely tart, floral, and tropical. The house drink at many restaurants and food trucks.

drinks.name: Mai Tai
instructions: The Mai Tai is the iconic tiki cocktail -- forever linked to Hawaiian beach bars
Shake aged rum, orange curacao, orgeat, and fresh lime juice with ice
Strain into a rocks glass filled with crushed ice
Float dark rum on top
Garnish with a mint sprig and lime wheel
Invented by Trader Vic (Victor Bergeron) in Oakland, California in 1944
The Royal Hawaiian Hotel on Waikiki Beach popularized it as THE Hawaiian drink
A real Mai Tai has NO pineapple juice and NO grenadine -- those are tourist bar additions
Orgeat (almond syrup) is what gives a Mai Tai its distinctive nutty sweetness
drinks.description: Iconic tiki cocktail -- Mai Tai, aged rum with orange curacao, orgeat (almond syrup), and fresh lime, floated with dark rum. Invented by Trader Vic (1944). The Royal Hawaiian Hotel popularized it. A real Mai Tai has NO pineapple juice or grenadine -- those are tourist additions.

drinks.name: Blue Hawaii Cocktail
instructions: The Blue Hawaii is the colorful Hawaiian cocktail -- the drink that matches the ocean
Shake light rum, blue curacao, pineapple juice, and sweet and sour mix with ice
Strain into a hurricane glass or tiki mug
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and maraschino cherry
Created by Harry Yee at the Hawaiian Village Hotel (now Hilton) in Waikiki in 1957
Blue curacao gives the drink its vivid blue color
Sweet, tropical, and photogenic -- the quintessential tourist cocktail
drinks.description: Colorful Hawaiian cocktail -- Blue Hawaii, rum with blue curacao and pineapple juice. Created by Harry Yee at the Hawaiian Village Hotel in Waikiki (1957). Sweet, tropical, and photogenic. The drink that matches the ocean.

drinks.name: Hawaiian Sun Drinks
ingredients: Hawaiian Sun canned juice (various flavors: guava, lilikoi, luau punch)
instructions: Hawaiian Sun is the local canned juice brand -- a cultural institution
Flavors include guava nectar, passion orange, luau punch, and lilikoi
Every school lunch in Hawaii includes a Hawaiian Sun juice
The small 6oz cans are iconic -- recognizable by their fruit-themed labels
Hawaiian Sun has been operating since 1952
Mainland transplants and tourists bring cases home in their luggage
drinks.description: Hawaiian cultural institution -- Hawaiian Sun canned juice. Flavors: guava nectar, passion orange, luau punch, lilikoi. Every school lunch includes one. The small 6oz cans with fruit labels are iconic. Operating since 1952. Tourists bring cases home in luggage.

drinks.name: Kona Coffee
ingredients: Kona coffee beans (100% Kona -- from the Kona Coffee Belt on the Big Island)
Optional: coconut creamer, macadamia nut syrup
instructions: Kona coffee is Hawaii's world-famous coffee -- grown on the slopes of Hualalai and Mauna Loa
Brew 100% Kona coffee (not a "Kona blend" which can be as little as 10% Kona beans)
The Kona Coffee Belt: a narrow strip on the western slopes of the Big Island with perfect growing conditions
Volcanic soil, morning sun, afternoon clouds, and gentle rain create ideal coffee conditions
The flavor: smooth, low-acid, with notes of chocolate, brown sugar, and macadamia
Kona coffee is one of the most expensive coffees in the world
Coffee was brought to Hawaii by Chief Boki in 1828
Can be served with coconut creamer or macadamia nut syrup for a Hawaiian twist
drinks.description: Hawaii's world-famous coffee -- Kona, grown on the slopes of Hualalai and Mauna Loa on the Big Island. Volcanic soil, morning sun, afternoon clouds. Smooth, low-acid, with notes of chocolate and macadamia. One of the most expensive coffees globally. Coffee arrived in Hawaii in 1828.
